subsystems.name: Delivery pods
subsystems.role: small ground robots that carry individual parcels or food orders the last few kilometres.

subsystems.name: Trunk and hub layer
subsystems.role: moves goods in bulk between neighbourhood hubs, where pods pick them up.

subsystems.name: Coordination layer
subsystems.role: lets hundreds of pods share routes, kerbs and charging points without a central dispatcher for every decision.

subsystems.name: Street interface
subsystems.role: the physical places where pods stop, load and park.

subsystems.name: Remote supervision
subsystems.role: humans watch the fleet and take over when a pod is stuck.

subsystems.name: Standards and access rules
subsystems.role: without shared pod dimensions and data formats, operators cannot hand goods to each other.

buildSteps.title: Fix a pod standard
buildSteps.detail: Agree common footprint, weight limit, tote sizes, battery voltage and a data format, so any operator's pod can carry any operator's parcel. This is the step that makes a city-wide mesh possible at all.

buildSteps.title: Build neighbourhood hubs
buildSteps.detail: Convert underused buildings or car parks within a few kilometres of homes into micro-depots where trunk vehicles unload and pods are charged and dispatched.

buildSteps.title: Instrument the kerb
buildSteps.detail: Map and digitise loading bays, footpath widths, crossings and steep slopes, then add sensors or beacons so pods know where they may stop.

buildSteps.title: Train the swarm in simulation
buildSteps.detail: Run millions of simulated deliveries on a digital twin of the city to test routing, congestion and kerb allocation before any real robot appears.

buildSteps.title: Pilot in one district
buildSteps.detail: Deploy a few dozen pods in a single walkable neighbourhood, with remote supervisors, to learn failure modes and public reaction.

buildSteps.title: Connect hubs into a mesh
buildSteps.detail: Link multiple districts with trunk movements so goods can travel across the city by being handed from pod to van to pod.

buildSteps.title: Scale and standardise operations
buildSteps.detail: Move from company-specific fleets to shared depots and interoperable pods, with cities setting access rules.

buildSteps.title: Harden for all weather and demand
buildSteps.detail: Solve rain, snow, flooding, hills, crowded markets and peak days, which are what break pilots.

prerequisites.why: sidewalk robots operate today but only in limited areas, at low speed, with remote help when stuck.
multi-agent planning works in simulation and small fleets; thousands of units sharing kerbs is untested.
without shared pod and tote dimensions, goods cannot pass between competing fleets.
cities rarely hold accurate, machine-readable data on loading bays, footpaths and crossings.
a city-wide fleet needs many small, low-power charging points on kerbs and in depots.
who pays when a pod blocks a footpath or collides is largely unsettled.

pathway.milestone: sidewalk delivery robots and autonomous vans in limited districts
pathway.unlocks: real data on navigation, public acceptance and last-mile cost.

pathway.milestone: shared micro-depots and digital kerb management in a handful of cities
pathway.unlocks: pods can be loaded and charged outside company silos.

pathway.milestone: one city district where pods, vans and lockers are coordinated by common software
pathway.unlocks: proof that a mesh beats individual fleets on cost and congestion.

pathway.milestone: open pod standards and cross-operator handover city-wide
pathway.unlocks: goods move between any carrier, the way parcels already move between postal networks.

pathway.milestone: cities where a large share of physical goods are moved autonomously
pathway.unlocks: quieter, less congested streets — but only if energy, safety and public consent all hold.
